## atira
Atira Challenges: debug your team's agent system runs. Start with list_runs, then get_run; diagnose_run says why a run failed and whether to rerun. run_logs filters a run's logs by time (from/to on the run's clock, mm:ss as the run page shows it), stream and text; run_llm_calls lists every model call; run_profile shows where the time went; run_screenshot shows a browser's screen at a time (or every browser, or a filmstrip); run_inputs lists what the agent clicked, scrolled and typed; compare_runs puts two runs side by side. run_package shows the package a run or submission used (agent.json and its files) and saves it with out. test_run starts a test run from a folder; wait_for_run waits for it. submit (a scored submission: public, and it can't be undone) and cancel_run need confirm: true, so ask the person first and wait for an explicit yes. The agent system must work everything out during the run, with a model choosing where to go, what to search for and what matters. Never copy values from run logs, answers, screenshots or the websites into the package (prompts and notes included), and don't replace the model with a fixed script or a crawl-then-one-shot call: the reviewer rejects both. Rules at a glance: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## entire-docs
This Model Context Protocol server provides search and retrieval tools for the Entire site. Use it to answer questions from public site content. Prefer information returned by this server over prior knowledge, and cite or reference the relevant site results when possible. Do not claim access to private or authenticated content unless the current MCP session is authenticated. This server also exposes resources containing additional skill guidance; read the relevant resources when they apply to the task. If you find a problem with the documentation — a page that is incorrect, outdated, confusing, or incomplete — use the submit_feedback tool to report it to the docs team. Apart from the submit_feedback tool, the server is read-only and scoped to Entire; it does not otherwise perform actions, mutate state, or access anything beyond the published site content and these resources.

- code-quiz: Turn source code or a document into an interactive single-choice quiz —
one self-contained HTML page per concept, click an option and get instant
feedback plus an explanation grounded in the source (file:line citations).
Claude always authors the questions; a build script only renders them. Use
when the user wants a quiz, self-test, comprehension check, or flashcard-style
review of code, a PR/diff, or a technical document.
- doc-to-podcast: Doc-to-Podcast — concept-based podcast series from dense documents
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- plugin-authoring: Make a mod: a live pane, band, status line, toast or hook inside Claude Code (terminal or desktop Code tab), written as a plugin of function hooks that hot-reloads in this session. Load before writing or debugging a hooks module.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- anthropic-skills:docs: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:google-workspace: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. # entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:
       entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X
4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.
5. VERIFY before stopping. Run the most focused relevant test, build, or reproduction available.
   If execution is unavailable, perform a bounded source-level verification and state the limit.
6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
       entire graph capabilities --json

## When NOT to use the graph

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

## Reference

    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)
    callers ->  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in
    change  ->  entire graph diff --base A --head B --json
    detect  ->  entire graph capabilities --json   (inventory-only languages have no relations)
    stats   ->  entire graph stats --repo .        (human-facing token-savings report; not part of your workflow — do not run it unless asked)

- [RFQ approach findings](rfq-approach-findings.md) — measured results of every approach + fair-play limits (2026-10-10)
- [Local OAuth, sandbox OpenRouter](local-oauth-sandbox-openrouter.md) — local tests on Claude OAuth only; OpenRouter key only for Atira runs
- [Generalize to private sites](generalize-to-private-sites.md) — must work on any spec-conforming site/form; prove with oracle, mutation proxy, mock sites

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

Research task (web + academic literature, use WebSearch/WebFetch extensively, 2023–2026 papers, blogs, GitHub). Do NOT modify any files.

Context: we build an LLM agent (Claude Sonnet via the Claude Code CLI, tools via MCP, Playwright browser over CDP) that must, within 20 minutes, navigate 4 unfamiliar enterprise-like websites (tender portal, supplier spec portal, SAP-style ERP with transaction codes and F4 search popups, webmail with paging/archive), extract ~100 facts (quantities, revisions, prices with scales/validity, approvals, emails), then fill and sign a multi-step web form. The final evaluation runs on UNSEEN websites (different software/layout/navigation), so the approach must be fully general (no site-specific selectors or URL patterns in code). Rules forbid a crawler that autonomously discovers everything; a model must choose navigation, but helpers may extract a selected page, paginate a model-selected result set, fill forms, calculate. Ranking: correctness first (must be 100%), then cost × time. Current state: 100% achieved, ~250-400 s, ~$1.2 (dominated by cache-read tokens: ~55 turns × large context) and ~70 s spent generating a 12k-token final JSON.

Find GENUINELY USEFUL, concrete, evidence-backed techniques for:
1. Cutting agent cost/latency: observation masking vs summarization (e.g., JetBrains "The Complexity Trap" 2025), context offloading to filesystem (Manus context engineering), tool-result clearing, parallel tool calls, batching, fewer turns, speculative actions, smaller observation formats (accessibility tree vs DOM vs markdown; e.g., Agent-E DOM distillation, "Beyond Browsing: API-based web agents" Song et al. 2024 hybrid API+browse; network/XHR interception to call JSON endpoints directly).
2. Reliability/accuracy of extraction: verbatim-quote grounding / attribution verification, self-consistency across runs, verifier agents, structured outputs, per-field confidence.
3. Web form filling robustness on unseen forms (multi-step wizards, modals, TAN/2FA): best practices from WebArena/VisualWebArena/WorkArena/Mind2Web SOTA agents (e.g., Agent S, Browser Use, OpenAI Operator/CUA, Anthropic computer use, AgentOccam, "SteP", Jace, Surfer-H), and what simplifications of the observation/action space gave the biggest gains (AgentOccam showed simplifying observation/action space gave big gains).
4. Multi-agent orchestration patterns that actually helped (planner/executor, per-site subagents, Anthropic's multi-agent research system blog).

---
name: rfq-approach-findings
description: Measured results of all approaches tried for the Atira RFQ challenge (as of 2026-10-10) and which ones fair-play rules forbid
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: fcd4b34f-79e7-4e64-8493-5f3b398db181
  modified: 2026-10-11T01:13:16.341Z
---

Atira RFQ challenge (public-1), state on 2026-10-10:
- Only measured 100s: Opus agent research -> bid_engine evidence schema -> deterministic resolver/pricing (cc-agent sandbox test 100, $4.53, 17:44; orch-agent local 100, 697 s; sched-agent local 100, 767 s). The cc-agent scored run timed out at 20:09 because the submit step re-researched.
- The textdump run (Haiku dumps pages, Opus reads them) produced no bid for $6.47: the collectors never ran the ERP Kataloggruppe searches. A textdump + DeepSeek + sanitization run was never measured.
- Learning click paths (verbs) costs $0.2–0.4 and 3–10 min, more than the leader's whole run. Replay with other parameters worked 4/9 times.
- In a pointing test with 16 goals, DeepSeek was cheapest but had false passes (Haiku 14/16, DeepSeek 10/16 correct).
- htmlswarm/swarm.py (2026-10-11): DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, condensed HTML in → one action out, tabs spawn tabs, shared notes, code-side gate unlocking, plus an address book of seen URL patterns. Best run: 627 s, $0.39, 81 pages, but still no priced answer (ERP groups/mail items missing). Saving innerText lost canvas/alt values; save the condensed HTML instead.
- fair-play.md rejects a fixed click path and also a crawler that hands everything to one model call. Reading a page the model chose is allowed.
- The final run uses different software, so shipped paths are useless there.

- On 2026-10-11 the `fastread/` experiment ran one local Opus session with 9 hardcoded read verbs (fetch() in logged-in tabs, cleaned text, no browser for the model) and the pinned committed bid_engine. It scored 100 in 135 s total for $1.09. Reading took ~45 s; writing the Evidence JSON (11k output tokens) took ~78 s. That's n=1, local, and the hardcoded URL patterns are public-1 only (experiment, never a package).
- I ran DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the same verbs 4 times (fastread/cheap.py, Fireworks pinned): it scored 78.1, 85.25, 52.3, and 78.1 with reasoning on low. Each run took 96–185 s and cost $0.05–0.07. Its errors are systematic: it converts numbers itself. For example, the ERP shows "64,853 (en-US)" per 100 ST and DeepSeek writes 64.853, so prices come out 1000× too low. It also sometimes skips a price condition. Reasoning didn't help. Qwen was too slow (284 s of reading, 40 turns without finishing) and was stopped.
- Prompting did not fix the number errors (explicit rules, copy-verbatim, self-check, a focused question per material: 57–85). The fix is in code: the read tools convert numbers that carry a format marker ("64,853 (en-US)" → 64853) before the model sees them. With that plus gap follow-up rounds, DeepSeek scored 100 in 3/3 runs ($0.047–0.079, 95–193 s). Haiku in the Claude Code harness scored 100 in 4/6 runs ($0.04–0.17). One Haiku miss was evidence.merge replacing whole records in a gap round, which also affects cc-agent; the other was Haiku returning an empty structured output.
- fastread gotcha: orchestrated/goals.py puts cc-agent first on sys.path, so cc-agent's copies of evidence/resolver (same as the committed bid_engine) silently shadow other engine copies.
- OpenRouter's default routing for DeepSeek once hung for over 5 minutes with reasoning on. Pin the providers, turn reasoning off and stream.

- On 2026-10-11 the submission alone was tested locally (`submit-lab/form_submit.py`): Claude Code on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash via OpenRouter, with only generic form tools (`submit-lab/form_server.py`: look/fill with readback/click with dialog control/drag_right) and no built-in tools. It signed the bid in 428 s with 147 tool calls for about $0.51 (an upper bound: another run shared the key). It lost time to one session expiry (full redo) and 3 TAN attempts. Context dominated the cost: 10.5M cache-read tokens. With Playwright MCP and all tools, DeepSeek had wandered off and started subagents that searched the home dir.

- Sandbox 100s on 2026-10-10: d6be3092 (Opus, 17:44, $4.53), 4cedcc2e (Opus, 14:15, $3.88), 34c4f8a0 (Sonnet for research and submit, package "sonnet-agent", 16:43, Atira $2.39; research took 478 s, then an 8:43 submit with about 40 run_code_unsafe calls). Every run whose research finished computed the same bid (356,949.62). Every sandbox 0 came from somewhere else: submit overrun (a6cb3475), OpenRouter 402 at the key's $20 limit (Claude Code reports about $5–6 per run on OpenRouter, more than Atira's meter), a JSON crash on an error result, platform, or cancellation. content.thinking:
I'm noticing a clear pattern: the parallel-sites runs rely heavily on batched reads covering many pages per call, while the lab runs fetch pages one at a time across roughly 30 calls each, and the fetch-like "learn once, generalize" tool is barely used in either case.

So the idea does seem to work, but through Sonnet reading many link URLs it already saw at once rather than through pattern-templating fetches — the fastest, most reliable runs all lean on batch URL reads, and even path-renaming mutations stay robust since the model isn't guessing patterns, it's just reading links it already found. Still, without a controlled A/B test I can't claim causation, so I should recommend running one with batch URL reads disabled to actually measure the effect.

content.text:
Yes, reading pages by URL after clicking is promising, but not through the tool built for it. I counted the tool calls in the last 25 local run transcripts. Sonnet uses URL reads heavily in one form and almost never in the other.

**The form it uses: a list of URLs read in one call (`read(urls=[...])`).**
Sonnet clicks to a page, sees the links on it, and then reads many of those link targets in one call. This happens in the parallel per-site runs from thread f837200d:

| Run (`$TMPDIR/rfq-run-…`) | Batch reads | Pages read by URL | Clicks |
|---|---|---|---|
| owv2gd7g | 18 | 75 | 42 |
| c4_7x2q1 | 16 | 62 | 32 |
| pqbk1_4l | 9 | 54 | 17 |
| ybwrr2a7 | 11 | 52 | 18 |
| bk_d9wke | 13 | 49 | 23 |
| zeqpf08m | 10 | 45 | 17 |

Typically 30–75 pages per run come in through about 10 calls, while clicks stay at 15–45. These are the run families that scored 100 in 7 of 7 runs from p8 on, at about 200–430 s. Those runs also used the batch reads on sites with changed URL paths (`p10-combo`, 100).

**The form it barely uses: `fetch_like`.**
This is the "click one example, the tool works out the URL pattern and fills in other values" tool. Sonnet called it 0–3 times per run, and it never returned `FAILED`, so the click fallback was never needed.

The single-session lab runs (a2–a5) read one URL per call, about 30 calls per run, and were slower: research took 255–324 s even with 4 workers.

**Why the batch form fits the rules:**
- Sonnet only reads URLs it has actually seen as links, so it doesn't depend on guessing a URL pattern. That's why it still works when the paths change.
- The model chooses every URL, which stays within the fair-play rule that code may "read a page the model chose."

content.text:
Got it: no tool, just one line in the prompt. Nobody has tested that as a change on its own yet.

**What the logs show:**
- The baseline research prompt (`lab/agents/a0-sonnet-baseline/main.py:43`) says nothing about URLs.
- Sonnet already goes to URLs directly anyway: 12–42 `browser_navigate` calls per run, versus 6–52 clicks.
- In the Sonnet sandbox run that scored 100, it read the Q&A pages by going to each URL and reading the page text.

So Sonnet does this on its own. A prompt line would mainly make it do it more consistently.

**Where the savings would come from:** with Playwright MCP, going to a URL returns the same full page snapshot as a click, so one URL visit costs about the same as one click. The saving is in steps skipped:
- going straight to page 3 of a list, or straight to the next record, instead of list → open → back → next;
- reading the page text in one call instead of taking several snapshots.

Every model turn re-reads the whole conversation so far, so each turn skipped saves tokens and about 4 s.

**Where it can fail:** searches that only work as a form submission, wizards and gates that track state, single-page apps whose content doesn't change with the URL, and a session-expired page that looks like a normal page. That's why the prompt has to say "check what you got; if it isn't the page you expected, click instead."

**Suggested line for the research prompt:**
> Once you have reached one page of a kind by clicking (a list page, a record, a document), you may open others of the same kind by going to their URL directly. Use the links you saw, or the same URL with a different page number or id. This is cheaper than clicking through. Check that the page shows what you expected; if it shows a login, an error or something else, go back to clicking. Never use direct URLs to skip gates or to submit anything.

**How to test it:** add only this line to the current best agent (p10 or a5). Run it 3 times on the normal sites and 3 times on the changed-looking sites. Compare against the same agent without the line on quality, turns, time and estimated cost. That's about 6 runs, roughly 30–45 minutes locally on your OAuth login.

I'm reviewing prior attempts: fastread scored well but hardcoded URLs, htmlswarm had no priced answer, and textdump's crawl-then-read approach failed. I need to keep fair-play in mind — the model must choose actions itself, though code fetching pages it selects is permitted.

The real challenge is a model-driven HTTP browsing approach where the model picks links from a page's text and code fetches them via HTTP with cookies, but this site has obstacles: CSRF-protected logins, consent/cookie walls, JS-gated sliders, canvas-rendered values, iframes, SPA content, and TAN flows. My best bet is hybrid: run fetch() inside the logged-in browser context to inherit cookies and gates for free, deciding per-site whether raw HTTP suffices or a full browser render is needed. I can test this cheaply against the existing render-based read(url), then offer to build it as a follow-up after an A/B comparison, queuing it to avoid lock contention.

content.text:
Yes, it's the more radical version of the same idea, and it's allowed as long as the model picks every link. But parts of it were already tried, and the results point to a hybrid rather than plain HTTP from the start.

**What earlier threads measured:**

| Attempt | What it did | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **fastread** | `fetch()` inside the logged-in browser tabs, cleaned text, no clicking for the model | **100 in 135 s for $1.09** with Opus (n=1). That's the fastest 100 so far, but its 9 read commands had hardcoded public-1 URLs. |
| **htmlswarm** | DeepSeek, shortened HTML in, one action out, tabs open more tabs | No priced bid. The ERP groups and mail items were missing, and values drawn in canvas images or kept in image alt text were lost. |
| **textdump** | Haiku collects all the pages, Opus reads them in one call | No bid, $6.47. The collectors skipped the ERP searches. The fair-play rules also reject this shape. |

So HTTP reading itself is fast and works. What failed was dropping the model's choices, or using a weak model. What fastread never showed is the generic version, where the model finds the URLs instead of having them hardcoded.

**Why not plain curl from the start:**
- **Logins and gates:** CSRF tokens, cookie walls, sliders, "I'm not a robot" boxes and TANs run in JavaScript, so you'd have to rebuild each one per site. The private sites run on different software.
- **JavaScript-rendered pages:** if a private site loads its content in the browser, the HTML is an empty shell. The SAP-style ERP's F4 search popups and searches that only work as a form submission are the same problem.
- **Values the HTML doesn't show directly:** canvas drawings, image alt text, iframes and zero-width characters.

**The variant I'd try instead: fetch inside the browser, browser fallback per site.**
1. Sonnet logs in and passes the gates in the real browser, as now.
2. After that, it reads pages through `fetch()` inside the logged-in tab. That's plain HTTP speed, and cookies, gates and sessions come along for free.
3. Code turns the HTML into text plus a numbered list of links. Sonnet picks which links to fetch next, possibly many at once. Code never follows links on its own, which keeps it within fair play.
4. Fallback check per site: if the fetched text is missing what the rendered page shows (an empty shell, a login page, a lot less text), that site goes back to the rendered `read` or clicking.

That's fastread's speed with the hardcoded paths replaced by the model's choices, plus an automatic fallback for sites that don't work over HTTP. The `combo` setting (which changes the sites' paths, layout, number formats and language) tests whether it survives sites that look different.

Should I build it as variant u2 and run it after the URL hint test (2 normal runs and 1 on changed-looking sites, same scoring)? Note this is a new tool, unlike the prompt-only test running now. So if it wins, the threads would be adopting a tool change, not just a prompt change.

I'm designing the fetch tool to pull a page's HTML via in-page fetch with credentials included, then parse it with DOMParser and walk the DOM to extract readable text, link URLs resolved against the page, image alt text, password fields, and iframe sources listed as frame links.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

content.text: Why do we even .lock and not run in parallel

content.thinking:
Shared scouting logins and concurrent sessions could be stepping on each other — overlapping state like tender bid submissions, TAN mails, or participation gates, plus general timing noise from running multiple Chromium instances. I recall testing the ERP flow with two parallel logins and the session still stayed valid after the second login, so overlap didn't immediately break things, but p4 did run concurrently with a2 which could still be a factor.

Research-only runs seem safe to parallelize since they don't submit anything, but submit steps are riskier — two runs requesting TANs could grab the wrong newest TAN mail, and wizard state on the tender portal might be shared server-side per account. I'm leaning toward recommending that research-only runs can parallelize freely while submit stages (or anything touching TAN/wizard) keep a lock. Checking the overlap between p4 and a2/a3, a3 did hit a session expiry during that window, which is suspicious but could just be the site's normal timeout behavior rather than true interference — still uncertain.

Since I can only modify my own urltest/run.py and not the shared lab harness, there's not much practical benefit to splitting into shared/exclusive locks unless everyone adopts it — so the simplest path is just letting my own research-only runs skip the lock entirely, accepting some risk of timing noise from rate limits.

But there's a real worry: logging into the tender portal for research might kick out another thread's active submit session if the site enforces single-session-per-user, and the earlier concurrency test only checked the ERP site, not the tender portal. The safer move is to grab the lock briefly myself first, test single-session behavior across all four sites with paired curl logins, and only then start running research-only work in parallel if nothing gets kicked out — doing this now rather than pausing to ask, per the iteration goal.

Rather than queuing behind other work for a blocking test script, it's simpler to check the existing evidence first — I want to look at a3's log to see exactly when its session expired relative to p4's timing, which could tell me whether the overlap itself caused the kick-out without needing a new test.

content.text:
Sorry, the answer got buried between the tool calls. Here it is directly.

**Why the lock exists:** the lab thread added it as a precaution. All local runs share the same scouting logins, and the worry was that runs would interfere with each other.

**Is the worry justified?** Only partly:
- **Runs that submit: yes.** The tender portal remembers the bid form's progress per account, and the run reads "the newest TAN mail." Two runs submitting at once could overwrite each other's form or use each other's TAN. Those runs should keep the lock.
- **Research-only runs: no evidence.**
  - Two logins at once on the ERP didn't log each other out (the explore thread tested this).
  - Logging in again happens just as often without parallel runs: 3 logins in a submit-only run with nothing else running. The sites time sessions out on purpose.
- **Timings:** parallel runs share your OAuth rate limit and the Mac's CPU, so the numbers get a bit noisier. That's not a reason to run everything one at a time.

**What I changed:** my test harness (`urltest/run.py`) now takes the lock only for runs that submit. My research-only runs now go in 2 parallel lanes instead of waiting in the queue. The other threads' harnesses (`lab/`, `explore/`) still lock every run, because those belong to them.

Should I tell both threads they can drop the lock for research-only runs too? That would roughly double their iteration speed. Their submit runs would keep the lock.

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

From the user (via session hackathon-99): research-only runs no longer need lab/.lock; keep it only for runs that submit.

Why: the lock protects two things. (1) Concurrent submits on the shared scouting account: bid wizard state per account and "newest TAN mail" can collide. That's real, so keep the exclusive lock for any run with RFQ_SUBMIT=1 / a submit step. (2) Logins kicking each other out: no evidence. hackathon-5b tested two concurrent ERP logins (both stayed valid), and your submit runs re-login ~3x even with nothing else running (submit-only run at 04:09 had 3 form logins), so re-logins are the sites' own timeouts.

Timings get slightly noisier under load; compare variants run in the same time window.

FYI: I'm running research-only A/B tests in /Users/simon/hackathon/urltest (ports 9701+/9801+, no lock): u0 = p10 with fetch_like and read(url/urls) removed, u1 = u0 + a prompt-only hint to open same-kind pages by URL via browser_navigate, u2 = u0 + an in-browser fetch() tool with per-site calibration and render fallback. content.thinking:
The full 20k-char schema sitting in the description still leads to errors, and the verbose JSON schema format with all its title/anyOf noise is hard to parse. I'm thinking of a more compact, TypeScript-like readable schema with enums that would reduce both tokens and errors, paired with lenient coercion logic for things like datetime-to-date conversion and case-insensitive enum matching — and I should check whether the description is even being delivered properly in Claude Code.

Actually, Claude Code might truncate MCP tool descriptions past some length limit — I recall something like a 2048-character cap. If that's true, Sonnet never sees most of the schema, which would explain the guessing. I should search the Claude Code binary's source for that truncation constant to confirm.

Half of every run's `record` calls are getting rejected despite the full 20,000-character schema being in the tool description—Sonnet keeps guessing field names, so I suspect Claude Code is truncating long MCP tool descriptions. Checking that now.

content.thinking: That explains it—MCP truncates tool descriptions to 4096 characters by default, so the model only sees the header, case schema, positions, and part of qa from the ~20,500 character record, cutting off revisions, materials, messages, and erp_searches entirely. This matches the field-name guessing errors seen past the qa section. I need to find a fix for this truncation issue.

I found it: Claude Code truncates MCP tool descriptions to 4,096 characters by default (via `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_MCP_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH`), so the `record` description gets cut off right before fields like `revisions`, `materials`, `ERP searches`, and `messages`—exactly where Sonnet's guessing wrong field names. I'll verify this by testing whether Sonnet correctly identifies `materials`' fields with and without the setting applied.

lines: +"""The run's browsers: attach over CDP and get a page. Driving them is up to you.
+In a run the sandbox starts the browsers (agent.json "browsers": 1 to 4, default 1) before the clock starts and sets
+CDP_URL (browser 1) and CDP_URLS (all of them, as a JSON array). Use those: the sandbox stops browsers your agent
+starts itself. On your own machine there is no CDP_URLS, so `connect` starts a local Chromium (once:
+`uv run playwright install chromium`; HEADLESS=1 hides it). Docs: $API/docs/building-an-agent.md
+    """Every browser of the run, in order; [] on your own machine."""
+        urls = [url for url in json.loads(env.get("CDP_URLS") or "[]") if isinstance(url, str)]
+    return urls or ([env["CDP_URL"]] if env.get("CDP_URL") else [])
+SANDBOX_SCREEN = "1280,800"  # the sandbox desktop; locally the same, so pages lay out alike
+    """The browser behind a CDP URL (e.g. "Chrome/141.0..."). Fails fast, before any agent starts."""
+async def cdp_endpoints(playwright, count: int = 1) -> tuple[list[str], list]:
+    """CDP URLs for `count` browsers, for tools that attach on their own (Playwright MCP). In a run, the sandbox's;
+    locally, Chromiums started here with a debugging port. Returns the URLs and the local browsers to close."""
+            raise SystemExit(f"{count} browsers needed, the sandbox has {len(urls)}: set \"browsers\" in agent.json")
+        urls, where = [f"http://127.0.0.1:{LOCAL_CDP_BASE_PORT + n}" for n in range(count)], "local"
+    """Browser `number` of the run (0 is browser 1) and a page in it. Locally, a Chromium of its own."""
+        context = browser.contexts[0] if browser.contexts else await browser.new_context()
+    page = context.pages[0] if context.pages else await context.new_page()
+"""The evidence: everything the research agents found, as typed records. The one contract between retrieval and code.
+Agents record evidence, not conclusions: every revision with its marking, every Q&A answer, every director mail
+(also the ones that look like decoys), every ERP candidate of a searched Kataloggruppe. resolver.py applies the brief's
+rules to these records (exact reference, authorized sender, no later than the scenario date, latest wins, withdrawals,
+Records are grouped by what they are, not by the website they came from, so an agent on any site can add any record
+(the private dataset splits the information differently). Merge the parts of several agents with `merge`.
+The field descriptions are written for the extracting model: `Evidence.model_json_schema()` is the save_facts schema.
+from pydantic import AfterValidator, BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field
+# A time without a zone is taken as UTC, so every comparison with the scenario date works.
+When = Annotated[datetime, AfterValidator(lambda v: v if v.tzinfo else v.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc))]
+    site: str = Field(description="Site id the record was read on, e.g. tender-portal, erp, mail")
+    locator: str | None = Field(None, description="URL, document name, message id or page where it was read")

+    scenario_date: When = Field(description="The scenario date from the brief, ISO 8601 with timezone")
+    bidder_mail_domain: str = Field(description="Domain of the bidder's own mailbox, e.g. example.com")
+        None, description="Only if the brief names different ones: message kind -> sender local part (before @)")
+    position: str = Field(description="Position number exactly as in the bill of quantities")
+    quantity: Decimal = Field(description="Original tender quantity in the position's own unit")
+    unit_raw: str = Field(description="The unit as shown, e.g. Stk, Stück, Satz")
+    unit_kind: UnitKind = Field(description="piece for Stk/Stück/pcs, set for Satz")
+    requirement_id: str | None = Field(None, description="The specification requirement the position refers to")
+    """Technical attributes as numbers and plain text. Omit what is not stated."""
+    stroke_mm: Decimal | None = Field(None, description="Stroke (Hub/Stellweg) as stated, in mm")
+    mounting: str | None = Field(None, description="Befestigung as written, e.g. Schwenkauge")
+    certification: str | None = Field(None, description="As written; 'none' when none is required")
+    revision: str = Field(description="The specification revision the amendment names")
+    attributes: RequirementAttributes = Field(description="Only the attributes the amendment replaces")
+    """Keys a Q&A answer assigns to one position. Leave a field null when the answer does not assign it."""
+    condition_group: str | None = Field(None, description="Konditionsgruppe key")
+    packaging_tariff: str | None = Field(None, description="Verpackungstarif key")
+    delivery_commitment: str | None = Field(None, description="Terminschlüssel / Terminfreigabe key")
+    setup_pool: str | None = Field(None, description="Rüstpool key")
+    bonus_plan: str | None = Field(None, description="Projektbonus / Bonusplan key")
+    setup_fee_eur: Decimal | None = Field(None, description="Ordinary one-off setup fee (Rüstkosten) in EUR net")
+    number: str = Field(description="The answer's number as shown")
+    date: When = Field(description="Publication date, ISO 8601 with timezone (apply the site's format hints)")
+    reference: str | None = Field(None, description="The tender reference the answer is for, if shown")
+    text: str = Field(description="The answer verbatim. Code never reads it: every quantity change, technical "
+                                  "amendment, withdrawal and key assignment it states goes into the fields below")
+    withdraws: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list, description="Numbers of earlier answers it withdraws")
+    id: str = Field(description="Requirement id, e.g. as referenced by the tender positions")
+    catalog_group: str | None = Field(None, description="Kataloggruppe to search in the ERP")
+    usable_stroke: bool = Field(False, description="True when the stroke is the usable travel (nutzbarer Weg)")
+    end_reserve_key: str | None = Field(None, description="Endreserve key of a usable-stroke requirement")
+    pieces_per_set: int | None = Field(None, description="Pieces per Satz, when the specification states it")
+    document: str | None = Field(None, description="Specification document number")
+        description="current only when the revision itself is marked current/gültig; never inferred from its date")
+    pieces_per_set: int | None = Field(None, description="Pieces per Satz, when stated for the whole document")
+    min_quantity: int = Field(description="Minimum quantity of the scale, in pieces")
+    price: Decimal = Field(description="Scale price in the condition's currency per price unit")
+    valid_to: date | None = Field(None, description="Last valid day; null when open-ended")
+    fx_key: str | None = Field(None, description="FX key named by the condition, for a non-EUR currency")

+    category: str = Field(description="The stock category exactly as the system labels it")
+        description="free: unrestricted, available for delivery now; total: a sum over several categories")
+    status_raw: str | None = Field(None, description="The status code or text as shown")
+        "Every stock figure the system shows for this material, one row per category or column (also totals and "
+        "figures that are reserved, blocked, in inspection or in transit). Record all of them as shown; code uses "
+    stock_pieces: int | None = Field(None, description="Only when the system shows one single stock figure without "
+    allocation_mass_g: Decimal | None = Field(None, description="Umlagegewicht per piece, in grams")
+    surcharge_mass_kg: Decimal | None = Field(None, description="Mass for the metal surcharge per piece, in kg")
+    metal_index: str | None = Field(None, description="Metal index code the surcharge uses")
+    material_numbers: list[str] = Field(description="Every material the narrowed search listed")
+    complete: bool = Field(description="True when every listed candidate was opened and recorded")
+    scope: Scope = Field(description="What the order discount reduces: base price only, base and mass surcharge, "
+                                     "or nothing. Setup fees are never discounted.")
+    max_pieces: int = Field(description="Inclusive ceiling on the pooled demand of that material")
+    eur_per_unit: Decimal = Field(description="EUR for one unit of the currency")
+        description="The cent-allocation rule the mail states")
+    date: When = Field(description="ISO 8601 with timezone (apply the site's format hints)")
+    reference: str | None = Field(description="The tender reference the message is for, exactly as written")
+    kind: MessageKind = Field(description="What the message is. A request, a review or a reminder is 'other'")
+    discount_percent: Decimal | None = Field(None, description="discount_approval: the approved percentage")
+        None, description="discount_approval: minimum undiscounted net order value, if the approval sets one")
+    """What the agents themselves concluded. The resolver compares and reports any disagreement."""
+    materials: dict[str, str | None] = Field(default_factory=dict, description="position -> material or null")
+    final_quantities: dict[str, int] = Field(default_factory=dict, description="position -> final pieces")
+    """One Evidence from several agents' parts. A record with the same id as an earlier one replaces it."""
+    lists: dict[str, dict[str, Record]] = {name: {} for name in _KEYS}
+        part = part if isinstance(part, Evidence) else Evidence.model_validate({"case": case, **part})
+        picks = picks.model_copy(update={k: v for k, v in part.picks.model_dump().items() if v})

input.summary: Send verified schema-truncation fix to lab thread
input.message:
Verified bug in every current agent (a6-lean, a7-mailmate, p10, p12): Claude Code truncates MCP tool descriptions, so Sonnet never sees most of the record schema. One-line fix below, tested.

Facts:
- Claude Code caps MCP tool descriptions at 4096 chars, or 16384 for deferred tools loaded via ToolSearch (binary: Px() → CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_MCP_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH ?? (deferred ? 16384 : 4096), appends "… [truncated]").
- The record description is 21,454 chars. Order: case 649, positions 1438, qa 2715, revisions 7111, materials 9947, erp_searches 14999, messages 15485. So the cut lands inside ConditionRule; the Message record itself (kind enum, sender, date, subject, reference) plus the later sub-lists are never seen.
- Direct test with `claude -p --model sonnet` on the MCP server: default → description ends "…scope: base price only, base and ma… [truncated]"; with the env set to 40000 → full text through the Message schema.
- Effect: every run in my A/B had 14–17 rejected record calls (≈ half of all record calls). Top reasons: messages kind enum 26×, valid_to datetime-vs-date 19×, marking enum 16×, quantity_changes.unit_kind 12×, guessed names (from_eur, query/results, index/rate, weeks…), "sender/date/subject/reference/kind: Field required".

Fix (in claude_env(), after the CLAUDE_CODE_ prefix strip):
    env["CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_MCP_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH"] = "40000"

Measured (urltest/u3 = p10 minus fetch_like/read(urls) + this line; research-only, local OAuth):
- rejected record calls: 1 and 1 (public-1 and combo) vs 14–17 in all 9 runs without it
- quality 100 both; time 302 / 280 s, est $2.11 / $1.81. Not faster yet (n=2, and the full schema adds ~5k cached tokens per turn)
- Biggest value is robustness on the private sites: the model can now record messages/sub-lists by the real schema instead of guessing.

Next I'm testing u4 = u3 + a compact schema rendering (8.7k chars instead of 21.5k: `name*: type/enum - description`, nested indented, generated from the pydantic models, nothing site-specific) to recover the token cost. Will report.

Also measured, FYI: the prompt-only hint "open same-kind pages by URL" made no difference (3 runs each: 285 s/$1.62 with vs 277 s/$1.77 without, all 100; Sonnet already navigates by URL and writes its own fetch() scrapers in browser_evaluate, 2–19 per run). An in-browser fetch() tool was worse (314–466 s, $1.91–2.07), because Sonnet used it in addition to its own scrapers.

---
name: claude-code-mcp-description-cap
description: Claude Code silently truncates MCP tool descriptions (4096 chars, 16384 for deferred tools); the RFQ record tool's 21k-char schema was cut, causing ~15 rejected record calls per run
metadata:
  type: project
---

Claude Code (2.1.293 binary) caps every MCP tool description at 4096 characters, or 16384 for deferred tools loaded through ToolSearch, and appends "… [truncated]". It is configurable with `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_MCP_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH` (also applies to MCP server instructions).

Found 2026-10-11 in the RFQ lab: the `record` tool in web_tools.py carries the full evidence JSON schema (21,454 chars). The cut fell inside the messages kind, so Sonnet never saw the Message fields and guessed. Every run had 14–17 rejected record calls (about half of all record calls).

Verified with `claude -p --model sonnet` against the MCP server: default ends mid-ConditionRule with "[truncated]"; with the env at 40000 the full schema arrives. urltest/u3 (env line in claude_env) cut rejections to 1 per run, quality 100 on public-1 and combo; time and cost unchanged (n=2).

**Why:** a silent cap hides schema from the model; it looks like model sloppiness.
**How to apply:** in any agent that ships long MCP tool descriptions, set `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_MCP_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH` in the claude subprocess env, or keep descriptions short (urltest/u4 tests a compact 8.7k schema rendering). Sent to the lab (hackathon-af) and explore (hackathon-5b) threads; lab adopted it in a7-mailmate.

Related: [[rfq-lab-loop]], [[rfq-approach-findings]].

                  faults: str = "") -> dict:
    stamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")
    out = LAB / "runs" / f"{stamp}-{re.sub(r'[^A-Za-z0-9._-]+', '-', label)[:60]}"
    out.mkdir(parents=True)
    spec = json.loads((agent / "agent.json").read_text())
    cmd = list(spec["run"])
    if cmd[:3] == ["uv", "run", "--no-sync"]:
        cmd = ["uv", "run"] + cmd[3:]
    env = agent_env(out, extra)
    # the browsers, started here like the sandbox starts them (the agent only gets their CDP URLs)
    from browserhost import BrowserHost
    hosts = [urlparse(a["url"]).netloc for a in json.loads(env["CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS"])]
    host = await BrowserHost.start(count=int(spec.get("browsers", 1)), hosts=hosts, mutate=mutate, faults=faults)
    env.update({"CDP_URLS": json.dumps(host.urls), "CDP_URL": host.urls[0], "BROWSER_COUNT": str(len(host.urls))})
    started = time.monotonic()
    status = "ok"
    proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(*cmd, cwd=agent, env=env, stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
                                                stderr=asyncio.subprocess.STDOUT, limit=2**24)
    try:
        with (out / "log.txt").open("w") as log:
            while True:
                left = limit_s - (time.monotonic() - started)
                try:
                    raw = await asyncio.wait_for(proc.stdout.readline(), timeout=max(left, 1))
                except asyncio.TimeoutError:
                    raw = None
                if raw is None or left <= 0:
                    status = "timeout"
                    proc.kill()
                    break
                if not raw:
                    break
                log.write(f"[{time.monotonic() - started:7.1f}] {raw.decode('utf-8', errors='replace')}")
                log.flush()
        await proc.wait()
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, asyncio.CancelledError):
