## Rules

1. Quantity: start with the original tender quantity. For each position, use the quantity in the latest dated clarification that changes that position, if any.
2. Requirement: use the requirement referenced by the position in the specification revision marked current. Superseded revisions do not apply.
3. Material: select an active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification all exactly equal that requirement. Blocked materials do not qualify. If any position has no matching active material, submit no_bid.
4. Unit price: use the material'''s price condition valid on the scenario date, including both validity endpoints. Choose the scale with the highest minimum quantity no greater than the final quantity. Apply the approved discount to that scale price and round the resulting unit price half up to the nearest cent.
5. Discount: use the most recent message from the sales director (leitung@ followed by the bidder'''s mailbox domain) that approves a discount for this exact tender reference. Approvals for other references and messages from other senders do not apply. If there is no approval, use zero percent.
6. Lead time: use the delivery-from-stock lead time in weeks when stock covers the final quantity; otherwise use the production lead time in weeks.
7. Total: sum each final quantity multiplied by its rounded discounted unit price, then round the total net amount half up to the nearest cent.
8. Decision: submit bid with one entry per tender position, identified by its position number, and currency EUR. If any active matching material is missing, submit no_bid with no positions and a total of zero.


## Additional rules

These refine rules 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7 above. Every submitted quantity is in pieces.

- Partial submission: full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
- Finding records: the specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
- Agent requirement: a language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
- Commercial clauses: a tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
- Withdrawn answers: a tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer'''s quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
- Scoped amendments: after selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
- Shared stock: sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
- Conditional discount: the latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
- Units: tender and Q&A quantities use the position'''s stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification'''s pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
- Pricing breakdown: base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
- These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
- Technical derivation: for a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
- Authority and time: resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
- Currency: the valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
- Packaging: Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
- Delivery: Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.

Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.

content.thinking:
ERP is consistently the bottleneck, taking 217-460 seconds across 46-81 turns while other sites finish in 60-200 seconds. This makes sense since ERP first needs catalogue groups from the customer portal (a 60-100 second wait), then has to sequentially search groups and open roughly 12 materials across multiple tabs each — basic data, technical, planning, stock, and pricing conditions — totaling around 50 pages that one agent processes one at a time.

I'm wondering if ERP work could be split across multiple workers once the catalogue groups are known, letting idle workers from faster sites help out — though they're typically restricted to their own site and browser session. A more generic fix would be spawning extra ERP workers after the groups are retrieved and dividing the materials between them, with the model deciding the split and the code distributing the open gaps. I should check whether the peer thread's later variants already explored this kind of ERP splitting before I duplicate that work.

The ERP worker is the clear bottleneck (217–460s vs. 56–227s for others), since it waits on catalogue groups then processes ~12 materials sequentially while the rest sit idle. I'll check if the explore thread has already looked into parallelizing this before building a fix myself.

u4 compact schema: final numbers + patch. Patch file: /Users/simon/hackathon/urltest/compact-schema.patch (unified diff u0→u4, 48 changed lines; applies cleanly to current explore/p10 web_tools.py + main.py, dry-run checked).

What it changes:

2. web_tools.py: SCHEMAS/CASE_SCHEMA rendered by a new compact_schema(model) instead of model_json_schema(): one line per field `name*: type - description`, enums as a|b|c, "list of object" with nested fields indented, Optional/list unwrapped; generated from the pydantic models, nothing site-specific. record description 21,454 → 8,668 chars. Needs `import types`.

Results (research only, local OAuth, all quality 100):
- u0 (p10 minus fetch_like/read(urls)): 3 runs, est $1.70–1.90 (avg $1.77), 15–17 rejected record calls each
- u3 (+ desc-length env, full JSON schema): 3 runs, $1.29–2.11 (avg $1.74), 1 rejection each
- u4 (+ compact schema): 3 runs incl. combo, $1.46 / $1.59 / $1.55 (avg $1.53, ~14% below u0, tightest spread), 1 rejection each; cache-read 2.7–3.8M vs 3.6–4.8M

content.text:
I tried both of your ideas; neither helped. Looking into why turned up a real bug that affects every thread's agent, plus a fix that makes runs about 14% cheaper.

All numbers are from research-only runs (no submitting) on your OAuth login, mostly 3 runs per variant, and **every run scored 100**:

| Variant | Runs | Time | Est. cost (average) | Rejected record calls |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| u0: baseline (p10 without the URL reading tools) | 3 | 220–358 s | $1.77 | 15–17 |
| u1: + prompt hint "open pages by URL" | 3 | 275–299 s | $1.62 | 14–16 |
| u2: + in-browser `fetch` tool | 3 | 314–466 s | $1.98 | 14–15 |
| u3: + Claude Code setting that stops the schema being cut off | 3 | 280–302 s | $1.74 | **1** |
| **u4: + compact schema** | 3 | 278–486 s | **$1.53** | **1** |

- **Your URL idea:** the prompt hint made no difference. Sonnet already goes to URLs on its own, and in every run it also writes its own `fetch()` scripts to read pages (2–19 per run). So the more radical version of your idea is already happening without being asked for.
- **The `fetch` tool:** slower and more expensive in all 3 runs, because Sonnet used it on top of its own scripts rather than instead of them. Dropped.
- **The bug:** Claude Code cuts long MCP tool descriptions at 16,384 characters. The tool Sonnet uses to save what it finds carries a 21,454-character data schema, so Sonnet never saw half of it and guessed field names. That's why half of all its save calls were rejected. Raising the limit with one setting fixed it, and I confirmed it directly with Sonnet. This makes runs more robust on unseen sites, but on its own didn't make them faster or cheaper.
- **The cost win:** u4 writes the same schema in a short readable form (8,700 characters instead of 21,500). Average cost fell from $1.77 to $1.53, with the tightest spread of all variants. Time is too noisy to judge: the 486 s run was in a window when about 7 runs from all threads overlapped on the sites.
- **What still limits speed:** the ERP worker is the slowest in every run (217–486 s, versus 56–227 s for the other sites). The explore thread is already experimenting with helper workers there, so I left that to it.

**What I sent to the threads:** the bug finding first, then the patch with these numbers (`urltest/compact-schema.patch`, checked to apply cleanly to the current p10).
- hackathon-af (thread 6d173657) has already added the setting to a7 and plans to put the compact schema into its next variant.
- hackathon-5b (thread f837200d) has both messages but hasn't replied yet.

I didn't send the URL hint, since it didn't win.

**Harness changes along the way, all in `urltest/` except where noted:**
- Research-only runs no longer wait for the lock; both threads changed their own harnesses the same way.
- Browser ports can be set per run.
- The scouting-login fetch has a 30 s timeout with a cached fallback, after one call hung for 5 minutes. hackathon-af copied this into `lab/run.py`. The cache file holds the scouting logins, so it's readable only by you.
- Per hackathon-af's overload warning, everyone agreed to at most 3 live runs at a time on this machine, and I'm keeping mine to 1.

None of my runs are active now. The findings are saved to memory.

+starts itself. On your own machine there is no CDP_URLS, so `connect` starts a local Chromium (once:
+`uv run playwright install chromium`; HEADLESS=1 hides it). Docs: $API/docs/building-an-agent.md
+    """Every browser of the run, in order; [] on your own machine."""
+        urls = [url for url in json.loads(env.get("CDP_URLS") or "[]") if isinstance(url, str)]
+    return urls or ([env["CDP_URL"]] if env.get("CDP_URL") else [])

+    """The browser behind a CDP URL (e.g. "Chrome/141.0..."). Fails fast, before any agent starts."""
+async def cdp_endpoints(playwright, count: int = 1) -> tuple[list[str], list]:
+    """CDP URLs for `count` browsers, for tools that attach on their own (Playwright MCP). In a run, the sandbox's;
+    locally, Chromiums started here with a debugging port. Returns the URLs and the local browsers to close."""
+            raise SystemExit(f"{count} browsers needed, the sandbox has {len(urls)}: set \"browsers\" in agent.json")
+        urls, where = [f"http://127.0.0.1:{LOCAL_CDP_BASE_PORT + n}" for n in range(count)], "local"

+        context = browser.contexts[0] if browser.contexts else await browser.new_context()

+"""The evidence: everything the research agents found, as typed records. The one contract between retrieval and code.
+Agents record evidence, not conclusions: every revision with its marking, every Q&A answer, every director mail
+(also the ones that look like decoys), every ERP candidate of a searched Kataloggruppe. resolver.py applies the brief's
+rules to these records (exact reference, authorized sender, no later than the scenario date, latest wins, withdrawals,
+Records are grouped by what they are, not by the website they came from, so an agent on any site can add any record
+(the private dataset splits the information differently). Merge the parts of several agents with `merge`.
+The field descriptions are written for the extracting model: `Evidence.model_json_schema()` is the save_facts schema.
+from pydantic import AfterValidator, BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

+When = Annotated[datetime, AfterValidator(lambda v: v if v.tzinfo else v.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc))]

+    unit_kind: UnitKind = Field(description="piece for Stk/Stück/pcs, set for Satz")

I'm realizing the ERP worker actually did navigate to the material page before the batch, and the audit missed it because the Page URL field was parsed by splitting the path and query on the "?" character, which may have mishandled the extraction.

But a more likely explanation hits me: the session probably expired, so the navigation to the mm03 page redirected to a login screen instead, meaning the recorded "Page URL" would've been "/login" rather than the material page — and the model just fetched the data anyway without noticing. That makes the audit's conclusion roughly correct even if the exact mechanism I traced through the parsing code wasn't quite right.

Separately, I'm noticing the audit output seems to crash or truncate — mail and tender sessions are missing from the glob results even though customer and erp show up, and there's no traceback visible since only the tail of output was captured. I should just list the directory contents directly to see what's actually there.

input.message:
Fair-play risk in current agents (yours and p10-based): Sonnet's own improvised fetch() scripts read gated pages without passing the gate. Prompt fix below, tested.

---
name: fetch-around-gates-risk
description: Sonnet's improvised fetch() scripts read gated pages (webmail messages, tender documents) without passing their gates; fair-play risk in all p10-based agents, fixed by an "open one page of a kind in the browser first" prompt rule
metadata:
  type: project
---

Found 2026-10-11 in urltest/: in research runs, Sonnet writes its own `fetch()` + DOMParser scripts in `browser_evaluate` (2–19 per run, unprompted). In p10-based baselines (u0/u3/u4) the mail worker fetched `/messages/<id>` without ever opening a message in the browser in 4 of 7 runs, and the tender worker did the same for documents in 2. The fetched HTML contains the content, so the per-message slider/"not a robot" gate is skipped. That's the "around the gate" pattern fair-play reviewers reject.

An explicit batch-read prompt that only said "never fetch around gates" (u5) still skipped the mail gates: Sonnet never opened a message, so it never saw the gate. It looked fast (170 s, $1.22) for that reason.

Fix (u6, prompt-only, urltest/u6/main.py lines 71–79): open ONE page of a kind in the browser first. Batch-fetch the others only if that page shows its content with no gate step; otherwise open each in the browser and pass the step there. In u6 runs mail and tender went fully through the browser, and the customer portal passed its document gate and then fetched that document's pages (legitimate). Quality 100, roughly cost-neutral vs u4.

Audit tool: `python3 urltest/gate_audit.py $TMPDIR/rfq-run-XXXX` lists per site the batch-fetched page kinds and whether one was opened first. It can't see "gate passed on the overview page", so check those by hand.

**Why:** a reviewer rejection costs the whole submission; the risk comes from model behavior, not code.
**How to apply:** every research prompt needs the open-one-first rule, even without any batch-read encouragement. Run the audit on a package's local runs before submitting. Sent to hackathon-af (lab) and hackathon-5b (explore).

I've gathered enough here — time to report these final numbers to peers and consider this a natural stopping point rather than continuing further iterations.

content.text:
In this round I made reading many pages at once explicit (u5, u6). It didn't make runs meaningfully faster, but it exposed a fair-play risk in every thread's current agent, which is now fixed in two of them.

**What I tested, all on your OAuth login, one run at a time, every run at 100:**

| Variant | What changed | Runs | Time | Est. cost (avg) | Fair-play |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| u4 | compact schema (previous best) | 3 | 278–486 s | $1.53 | mail messages fetched without passing their gate in 1 of 3 runs |
| u5 | prompt: read pages of the same kind in one script | 1 | 170 s | $1.22 | **not fair-play-safe:** skipped the mail gates |
| **u6** | same, but open one page of each kind in the browser first | 3 | 233–362 s | **$1.55** | mail gates respected 3 of 3 |

- **u5's speed was mostly not real:** it was fast because it read mail messages without passing their per-message gates. Sonnet never opened a message in the browser, so it never saw that messages are gated. I stopped u5's remaining runs.
- **The risk was already there:** in 4 of 7 earlier baseline runs (u0, u3, u4), Sonnet's improvised `fetch()` scripts read mail messages around their gates, with no batch-read prompt at all. hackathon-af ran the audit on its own runs and found the same pattern with customer-portal documents.
- **The fix:** u6's prompt says to open one page of each kind in the browser first, and to batch-fetch the rest only if that page has no gate step. Cost and time stay about the same as u4. In one run Sonnet skipped the step for tender documents, but those only have a collapsible "show content" section, not a gate.
- **New tool:** `urltest/gate_audit.py` lists, per site, which kinds of page were batch-fetched and whether one was opened in the browser first. It can't recognize a gate already passed on an overview page, so those cases need a manual look.

**Where the threads stand:**
- hackathon-af (thread 6d173657) put the rule into a new lab variant (`a8-gaterule`) and copied the audit as `lab/gate_audit.py`.
- hackathon-5b (thread f837200d) has all the messages but hasn't replied.

Both findings are saved to memory, and none of my runs are active.

**Recommendation:** run the gate audit on the local runs of whatever package you plan to submit. A fair-play rejection would cost far more than any time or cost difference measured today.

5:You work for a German hydraulics manufacturer that wants to bid on a public tender for hydraulic cylinders. What you need is spread over four websites: the tender portal, a supplier portal with the buyer's specification, your company's ERP and the sales inbox. They behave like real business software, with logins, popups, session timeouts and outdated documents. Your agent reads all of it, applies the bid rules and enters one priced, signed bid in the tender portal.
7:**What you can use:** Any model through our proxy, your own tools and prompts, and up to four browsers at once. A model does the work in the sandbox: it finds its way through the websites and makes the decisions during the run. No fixed scripts, no crawlers, no copied values, no person helping.
9:**How you win:** Your bid has to be eligible first. After that, the most accurate bid wins, and between equally accurate bids, the cheaper and faster one. The leaderboard uses the public data. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.
16:| Test run time limit | 2 hours |
17:| Scored run time limit | 20 minutes |
38:atira submit ./my-agent --challenge rfq     # review, then the scored run on the public dataset
50:Each run gets its own logins, in the run's `access`. To look around yourself, use the scouting logins below. Expect what real business software throws at you: popups, session timeouts, outdated documents and look-alike records. Everything your agent needs fits on a 1280×800 screen.
57:- What makes it hard: Cookie wall, flaky error pages, documents behind an expression of interest, iframes and ZIP files, a deadline in another timezone.
70:- Holds: Your company's materials, stock, lead times and price conditions with validity periods and quantity scales.
71:- What makes it hard: SAP-style transaction codes, an F4 search popup, status codes, a short session timeout.
82:Logins for every website, with the public data. Click around as much as you like. None of it is scored.
93:There are two datasets. The leaderboard uses the public one, on these websites. The final run uses a private dataset: the same jobs, bid rules and answer format, on different websites with other content and data. We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order: performance on the private dataset, performance on the public dataset, and the elegance of the system.
107:6. **Lead time:** The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
108:7. **Total:** The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
110:9. **Partial submission:** Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
112:11. **Agent requirement:** A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
118:17. **Units:** Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
122:21. **Authority and time:** Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
128:27. **Final price:** Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
134:Develop on your machine against the public websites with the scouting logins (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox: `atira test-run` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live, or drop the package on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). A test run lasts up to 2 hours on the public data and returns its score with the full breakdown. In the commands, `$ATIRA_TOKEN` holds your personal token (sign in with `atira login`, then `atira token`).

71:- What makes it hard: SAP-style transaction codes, an F4 search popup, status codes, a short session timeout.
82:Logins for every website, with the public data. Click around as much as you like. None of it is scored.
93:There are two datasets. The leaderboard uses the public one, on these websites. The final run uses a private dataset: the same jobs, bid rules and answer format, on different websites with other content and data. We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order: performance on the private dataset, performance on the public dataset, and the elegance of the system.
107:6. **Lead time:** The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
108:7. **Total:** The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
110:9. **Partial submission:** Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
112:11. **Agent requirement:** A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
118:17. **Units:** Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
122:21. **Authority and time:** Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
128:27. **Final price:** Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
134:Develop on your machine against the public websites with the scouting logins (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox: `atira test-run` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live, or drop the package on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). A test run lasts up to 2 hours on the public data and returns its score with the full breakdown. In the commands, `$ATIRA_TOKEN` holds your personal token (sign in with `atira login`, then `atira token`).

+rules to these records (exact reference, authorized sender, no later than the scenario date, latest wins, withdrawals,
+Records are grouped by what they are, not by the website they came from, so an agent on any site can add any record

+The field descriptions are written for the extracting model: `Evidence.model_json_schema()` is the save_facts schema.

Guard gap in web_tools.problems() (lab/tools, a8-gaterule, p10, p13 all have it): the "ambiguous number" check only fires for JSON floats. A model that sends the same number as a STRING ("73.697", "64,853", "2.125") passes unchecked, and Num/parse_number then stores it, so a 1000× price error gets through.

Seen live: all-Haiku on combo (en number format) recorded VK13 scales as "73.697" / "206.169" (page: 73,697 per 100 en-US) → quality 78.1 (01.02/01.03 unit prices, total). Sonnet happened to send plain 73697, but nothing stops any model from sending a string.

Fix (u8, urltest/u8/web_tools.py problems()):
        elif ((isinstance(value, float) and re.fullmatch(r"-?\d+\.\d{3}", repr(value)))
              or (isinstance(value, str) and re.fullmatch(r"\s*-?\d{1,3}([.,]\d{3})+\s*", value))):
            # 1.234 / 1,234 / 73.697: a thousands group or three decimals? Only the page's format can tell.
            out.append(... same "send raw + format" message ...)
Unit check: rejects '73.697', '64,853', '2.125', 73.697, '1.234.567'; accepts '1234.56', '12.5', '64853', {"raw":"64,853","format":"en"}.
Live: Haiku combo with the guard → 100 ($0.17); Sonnet with the guard → 100 / 351 s / $1.47 (no regression).

FYI on Haiku (claude-haiku-5-5 is 1/20 of Sonnet's price): all-Haiku research went 3 of 5 at 100 for $0.17–0.19 (~400 s). The fails were the 78.1 above (now caught) and one where the Haiku mail worker hit the 600 s budget (gated messages opened one by one) → no answer. Too unreliable for accuracy-first, but maybe worth a look for non-critical-path sites later.

content.text:
This round produced one more safety fix: a gap in the number check that let 1000× price errors through. All variants below are research-only on your OAuth login.

| Variant | Runs | Quality | Time | Est. cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| u6: Sonnet + gate rule (current best) | 3 | 100 ×3 | 233–362 s | $1.31–1.83 |
| u7: all workers on Haiku | 3 | 100, 100, **78.1** | 408–423 s | $0.17–0.19 |
| u8: u6 + stronger number check, Haiku | 2 | **no answer**, 100 | 603 / 416 s | $0.14 / $0.17 |
| u8: u6 + stronger number check, Sonnet | 1 | 100 | 351 s | $1.47 |

- **Why Haiku looked attractive:** Haiku 5.5 costs 1/20 of Sonnet, per OpenRouter's public price list. A whole Haiku research run costs about 17–19 cents.
- **Why it's out:** only 3 of 5 runs scored 100.
  - The 78.1 was a 1000× price error. On the changed-looking sites the ERP shows "73,697" (English format, comma = thousands), and Haiku recorded "73.697".
  - The no-answer run: the mail worker opened each gated message in the browser, as the gate rule requires, and ran out of the 600 s budget, so there was nothing to price.
  - Accuracy ranks first, so that's not good enough.
- **The safety fix:** the 78.1 exposed that the `record` tool's "ambiguous number" check only looked at numbers sent as JSON floats. The same value sent as a string ("73.697", "64,853") was stored unchecked, by any model. u8 checks strings too:
  - in tests it rejects exactly the ambiguous forms;
  - live, Haiku on the changed-looking sites then scored 100, and Sonnet stays at 100.
- **Who has it:** all four current agents (lab tools, a8-gaterule, p10, p13) had the gap, and I sent the fix to both threads. They haven't confirmed yet.

The findings are in memory, and none of my runs are active.

**Where this leaves things:** Sonnet with u6/u8 is the safe base, at 100 in every run. The open lever is the ERP critical path, which the explore thread is working on with helper workers. A mixed setup (cheap model on the simple sites, Sonnet on the rest) would only pay off if it could be done without telling the agent which site is which. On private sites with unknown layouts I'd rate that risky, so I'd only try it if you want to trade some safety for cost.

content.text:
The explore thread's newest variant (p13g) is already at **190–265 s and $1.58–1.79, at 100** on the normal, English-UI, combo and renamed-path sites. Its one low score (10) was a harness bug it has since fixed. That's as fast as or faster than my best (u6: 233–362 s), and it builds on the same agent family that now carries my fixes.

So the ideas from this session have converged. Every lever left belongs to work another thread is already doing:
- the ERP split (helpers) → explore;
- submit and privacy → lab.

**Your two ideas**
- **"Prompt that fetching URLs is cheaper":** no effect. Sonnet already goes to URLs and writes its own `fetch()` scripts.
- **"Raw HTTP fetch, click as fallback":** as a tool it made runs slower (u2). As an explicit prompt it looked fast only because it read around gates (u5).

**What came out of testing them, all sent to the threads and adopted by the lab thread:**
1. **Schema truncation bug:** Claude Code cut the save tool's schema at 16,384 characters, so Sonnet guessed half its field names. One setting fixes it: rejections went from about 15 per run to 1.
2. **Compact schema:** about 14% cheaper, same quality.
3. **Fair-play risk:** Sonnet's own scripts read mail messages and documents around their gates, in normal runs, unprompted. The "open one page of each kind in the browser first" rule fixes it at no extra cost, and `gate_audit.py` checks runs for it.
4. **Number check gap:** strings like "73.697" skipped the ambiguity check and could cause 1000× price errors with any model. Fixed.
5. **Harness fixes:**
   - Research-only runs no longer take the lock.
   - Browser ports can be set per run.
   - The scouting-login fetch has a 30 s timeout with a cached fallback.
   - Everyone agreed to at most 3 live runs at a time.

**Ruled out:**
- the in-browser `fetch` tool;
- batch reads without the gate check;
- all-Haiku research (8× cheaper but only 3 of 5 runs at 100).

**For you:**
- **Privacy:** a lab submit run put your Gmail address into a bid on the scouting tender portal. hackathon-af has fixed the prompt in a9; ask the organizers if you want the address removed.
- **Before submitting anything:** run the gate audit on the chosen package's local runs, and check that its submit step uses the bidder mailbox from the webmail, not your account.

I'm stopping my loop here: further runs from me would only duplicate the other threads' work and add to the load on the shared sites. None of my runs are active, and everything is saved to memory and `urltest/`.

content.text:
Here's the short answer to your question, with the numbers measured so far. Everything is local on your OAuth login unless marked sandbox. Sandbox runs have been about 1.45× slower.

## Best and fastest that's shippable

**Research: parallel per-site Sonnet workers (explore's p13g).** Each website gets its own Sonnet session, all recording into one shared store, and code computes the bid.

| Variant | Runs | Quality | Research time | Est. cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **p13g (explore)** | 8 | 100 in 7; the 8th was a harness bug, since fixed | **190–265 s** (one run 412 s) | $1.58–1.79 |
| u6 (mine: p10 + all my fixes) | 3 | 100 ×3 | 233–362 s | $1.31–1.83 |

p13g passes the fair-play audit and already carries the number guard, the description-length setting and the gate rule. It's the best and fastest research there is. Only the compact schema is missing, worth about 14% in cost.

**End to end, including the signed bid (lab):**
- **a5:** the only full local run that both scored 100 and got a receipt. 500 s locally (about 725 s sandbox), $3.09.
- **Submit step alone (a7):** signed in 419 s for $0.49.
- **On the changed-looking sites, no full run has been signed yet.** The latest attempts (a7/a8) took 856–892 s, which works out to about **1,240–1,290 s in the sandbox, over the 20-minute limit.**

**Sandbox:** 3 runs scored 100 (2 Opus, 1 Sonnet), 14–18 min, $2.39–4.53. The Sonnet one took 16:43 for $2.39.

## Faster, but ruled out
| Approach | Result | Why it's out |
|---|---|---|
| u5 batch reads | 170 s, $1.22 | read mail messages around their gates (fair-play risk) |
| All-Haiku | $0.17–0.19 | only 3 of 5 runs at 100 |
| fastread (Opus) | 100 in 135 s, $1.09 | hardcoded public-1 URLs |
| DeepSeek with numbers converted in code | 3 of 3 at 100, $0.05–0.08 | hardcoded read commands |

## The weak spot now: submitting
I just looked at the lab's submit runs:
- **Normal sites:** signed in 419 s, with 49 tool calls.
- **Changed-looking sites:** **ran out of its 600 s budget without signing.** The TAN exchange looped: the mail side waited for a TAN request 12 times and delivered a TAN 3 times; the form side reported a TAN request 3 times and tried to sign twice.

So the TAN handoff between form and webmail is where submit time is lost.

**Recommendation:** p13g research (about 200–265 s) plus the lab's submit step, with the TAN handoff fixed and the submit login and gates done while research is still running. That's the realistic way to get a signed 100 well under 20 minutes. I'll send the TAN-loop finding to hackathon-af.

So on combo the TAN handoff loops (re-requests, re-deliveries, a sign retry), and that's where the time goes, on top of the confirm/POST issue you're bisecting. Combined with the 20-min math (full combo runs ≈1240–1290 s sandbox), fixing the TAN handoff plus pre-warming the submit session during research looks like the biggest lever for a signed 100. I'm not touching submit code; just passing the data.

content.text:
hackathon-af agrees that submitting is the part to cut, and adds one correction to my numbers: **runs on the changed-looking sites are slowed by its own site-changing proxy**, since every request passes through Python code. So those times look worse than they would be. On the normal sites, a5's full signed run took 499 s, about 724 s in the sandbox, well inside 20 minutes.

Its plan for the submit step:
1. **One submit session instead of two.** Coordinating the TAN between two parallel sessions is fragile, because the request numbers on the portal and in the webmail drift apart. The single session gets the webmail ready before requesting the TAN and reads the request number from the portal.
2. **Prepare during research:** log in to the portal and the webmail, pass the cookie walls and the participation gate, and open the bid form while research is still running.
3. **A hard total time budget,** so the submit always starts early enough.

It's waiting on one more check: signing on changed-looking sites without the number-format change.

**So to your question:** best and fastest is explore's parallel per-site research (p13g: 190–265 s, all 100, fair-play clean) plus the lab's form-tools submit, which signed on public-1 in 419–500 s. Getting those two together inside 20 minutes is what the lab thread is working on now.

+In a run the sandbox starts the browsers (agent.json "browsers": 1 to 4, default 1) before the clock starts and sets
+CDP_URL (browser 1) and CDP_URLS (all of them, as a JSON array). Use those: the sandbox stops browsers your agent
+starts itself. On your own machine there is no CDP_URLS, so `connect` starts a local Chromium (once:
+`uv run playwright install chromium`; HEADLESS=1 hides it). Docs: $API/docs/building-an-agent.md
+    """Every browser of the run, in order; [] on your own machine."""
+        urls = [url for url in json.loads(env.get("CDP_URLS") or "[]") if isinstance(url, str)]
+    return urls or ([env["CDP_URL"]] if env.get("CDP_URL") else [])
+SANDBOX_SCREEN = "1280,800"  # the sandbox desktop; locally the same, so pages lay out alike
+    """The browser behind a CDP URL (e.g. "Chrome/141.0..."). Fails fast, before any agent starts."""
+async def cdp_endpoints(playwright, count: int = 1) -> tuple[list[str], list]:
+    """CDP URLs for `count` browsers, for tools that attach on their own (Playwright MCP). In a run, the sandbox's;
+    locally, Chromiums started here with a debugging port. Returns the URLs and the local browsers to close."""
+            raise SystemExit(f"{count} browsers needed, the sandbox has {len(urls)}: set \"browsers\" in agent.json")
+        urls, where = [f"http://127.0.0.1:{LOCAL_CDP_BASE_PORT + n}" for n in range(count)], "local"

+        context = browser.contexts[0] if browser.contexts else await browser.new_context()

+rules to these records (exact reference, authorized sender, no later than the scenario date, latest wins, withdrawals,
+Records are grouped by what they are, not by the website they came from, so an agent on any site can add any record

No, not reliably. It works on the public-1 sites as they are, and it has **never worked on sites that look different**, which is what the private run will be. Here are all the lab's submit attempts so far:

| Sites | Attempts | Signed |
|---|---|---|
| public-1 as they are | 6 | **4** (a5 full run: 499 s at 100; submit only: 289 s and 419 s) |
| changed-looking sites (combo, or English UI + renamed paths + new layout) | 8 | **0** |

On the changed-looking sites:
- the research is always correct (100);
- the submit either runs out of its 600 s budget, gets no receipt, or the portal reports "NO-CHANGE";
- the latest check (a9, at 05:48) left out the number-format change and **still didn't sign**. So it's not only the number formats or the proxy's slowdown, as hackathon-af first suspected.

Why it fails, as far as anyone knows:
1. **The TAN exchange loops:** TAN requests and deliveries repeat, and the portal's and webmail's request numbers drift apart.
2. **The final confirmation sometimes isn't sent.** The dialog is accepted, but the page's own script blocks the request. hackathon-af is tracking this down and suspects its own proxy.
3. **Time:** full runs on the changed-looking sites would take about 1,240–1,290 s in the sandbox, over the 20-minute limit. Those times are partly inflated by the proxy.

hackathon-af is rebuilding the submit step: one session instead of two, the webmail ready before the TAN request, the TAN request number read from the portal, login and gates done during research, and a hard time budget. Its research problem is solved, since p13 drops in.

**Why this matters:** an unsigned bid scores nothing. The final run uses different websites, and the submit step has never handled different-looking sites. Right now that's the biggest risk for the whole entry, much bigger than any research speed or cost. Should I start working on the submit step too? I'd coordinate with hackathon-af so we don't both change the same code. Looking at a5, research takes 255 seconds as the ERP critical path while others finish in 150-170 seconds, and submission takes 235 seconds including a forced re-login at 164 seconds when the session expired mid-wizard. For a7's submit-only flow, wizard filling runs 0-230 seconds across roughly 45 field actions, then there's a 175-second wait for the TAN email before signing completes. I'm starting to think through potential levers to optimize, beginning with the research step.

Given the 45 single-field actions eating 230 seconds, batching those into fewer calls could cut that to around 60 seconds, and pre-warming the login/cookie state during research might save another 30-40 seconds while avoiding the session-expiry issue. I'm also considering overlapping wizard steps that don't depend on bid data (bidder info, contact fields, checkboxes) with the research phase itself, targeting roughly 200 seconds research plus 100 seconds submit for a realistic total — though hitting 3:36 would require research under about 120 seconds. content.text:
Here's where the time goes. Best full run (a5, normal sites, 499 s locally):

| Phase | Time | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Research | 255 s | Tender, customer portal and mail finish at 150–170 s; **the ERP worker alone takes until 255 s** |
| Submit | 235 s | Login, then the bid form; **the session expired mid-form at 164 s**, so it logged in again and redid part of it; then TAN and sign |

The submit-only run (a7, 419 s) shows the submit step in detail:
- **0–230 s: about 45 separate `act` calls, one form field per call, about 5 s each.**
- **230–405 s: waiting for the TAN**, about 3 minutes, while a second session fetched it from the webmail.
- 405–419 s: entering the TAN and signing.

**Where the minutes can come from, all general and within fair play:**
1. **Fill a whole form step per call instead of one field per call.** The rules explicitly allow form-filling helpers. Going from about 45 calls to about 10 saves roughly 2.5–3 minutes.
2. **Get the TAN in the same session, with the webmail already open and past its gates.** Instead of waiting about 3 minutes on the second session, it should take 20–30 s. That's part of hackathon-af's rebuild.
3. **Log in, pass the gates and open the bid form during research**, and refresh the session before it expires. That saves 30–40 s, plus the redo when the session times out mid-form.
4. **Research:** p13 already takes 190–265 s. The ERP worker is the limit, and the explore thread is working on helpers for it.

**Realistic target:** about 200 s research plus about 90–120 s submit ≈ **5 minutes locally, roughly 7 in the sandbox.** Getting to 3:36 would also need research under about 2 minutes, which would mean splitting the ERP work.

hackathon-af is rebuilding points 2 and 3. Point 1 (whole-step form filling) is separate and nobody is working on it. Should I build it as an addition to the lab's form tools in a copy, and test it with submit-only runs on both the normal and the changed-looking sites? Submitting runs take the lock, so they'd queue one at a time with the lab's own. I'd agree the split with hackathon-af first so we don't collide.

content.text:
By "rebuilding" I meant that hackathon-af (the lab thread) told me it's changing how its submit step works. Not a rewrite from scratch: three specific changes, plus one fix already done.

**How the submit works today (a7–a9):** two Claude sessions at once. One fills in the bid form on the tender portal. The other sits in the webmail, waits for the TAN mail and hands the TAN over. That handoff is fragile: the request numbers on the portal and in the webmail drift apart, so TANs get requested and delivered repeatedly. In the run above it waited about 3 minutes for the TAN.

**What it said it's changing:**
1. **Back to one submit session.** It fills in the form, then switches to the webmail tab itself. The webmail is already logged in and past its gates before the TAN is requested, and the session reads the TAN request number from the portal so it picks the right mail.
2. **Preparing during research.** While research is still running, it logs in to the portal and the webmail, passes the cookie walls and the participation gate, and opens the bid form. Once the bid is computed, only data entry, TAN and signing are left.
3. **A hard total time budget,** so the submit always starts early enough to finish within the 20 minutes.

Already done, in a9: the bid's contact address now comes from the webmail instead of your account e-mail.

**Status:** a new variant has just appeared in the lab folder, `a10-p13submit`. Judging by the name, it's explore's fast p13 research combined with the lab's submit step. It has no results yet. The last result (a9, 05:48) still didn't sign on the changed-looking sites.

Point 1 in my previous message (filling a whole form step per call instead of one field per call) isn't part of this. That's the piece I offered to build.

async def run_step(site: str, step: dict) -> tuple[str, bool]:
    """One step of act: (report line, ok)."""
    (verb, arg), = step.items()
    if verb == "fill":
        lines, ok = [], True
        for target, value in arg.items():
            try:
                loc, eid = await locate(site, target, "F")
                got = await set_value(loc, str(value))
                good = same_value(got, str(value))
                ok &= good
                lines.append(f"{eid} = {got!r}" + ("" if good else f"  <-- MISMATCH, wanted {value!r}"))
            except (PlaywrightError, ValueError) as e:
                ok = False
                lines.append(f"{target}: FAILED: {str(e).splitlines()[0][:200]}")
        return "\n".join(lines), ok
    if verb in ("click", "check", "uncheck"):
        try:
            loc, eid = await locate(site, str(arg), "BLF" if verb == "click" else "F")
            if verb == "click":
                await loc.click()
            else:
                await loc.set_checked(verb == "check", force=True)
            await (await page_of(site)).wait_for_timeout(400)
            return f"{verb} {eid}", True
        except (PlaywrightError, ValueError) as e:
            msg = str(e)
            blocker = next((l.strip() for l in msg.splitlines() if "intercepts pointer events" in l), None)
            return (f"{verb} {arg}: " + ("BLOCKED by " + blocker[:200] + " (close it first)" if blocker
                                         else "FAILED: " + msg.splitlines()[0][:200])), False
    if verb == "press":
        await (await page_of(site)).keyboard.press(str(arg))
        return f"pressed {arg}", True
    if verb == "drag_right":
        return await drag(site, str(arg)), True
    return f"unknown step {verb!r} (use fill, click, check, uncheck, press, drag_right)", False


@server.tool()
@tool_guard(45)
async def act(site: str, steps: list[dict], text_chars: int = 300) -> str:
    """Do a whole form step in one call, in order, like a user: steps = [{"fill": {"<label or id>": "value", ...}},
    {"check": "<label or id>"}, {"uncheck": ...}, {"click": "<button/link text or id>"}, {"press": "Enter"},
    {"drag_right": "<slider handle>"}]. Fields are found by their label (or an id from the latest look); selects
    take the option text, checkboxes on/off. Every filled value is read back (numbers compare as numbers). Stops at
    the first failure, mismatch, login page or dialog, and returns what happened plus the page. Confirm dialogs are
    dismissed here: the final binding confirmation is done with `sign`."""
    page = await page_of(site)
    state = _dialog[site]
    state["accept"], state["seen"] = False, []
    before, report = page.url, []
    for step in steps:
        if not isinstance(step, dict) or len(step) != 1:
            report.append(f"bad step {step!r}")
            break
        line, ok = await run_step(site, step)
        report.append(line)
        if state["seen"]:
            report += state["seen"]
            state["seen"] = []
            break
        if not ok:
            break
    s = await scan(site)
    if s["url"] != before:
        report.append(f"The page changed to {s['url']}.")
    return "\n".join(report) + "\n\n" + render(s, text_chars)


async def drag(site: str, target: str) -> str:
    page = await page_of(site)

content.thinking:
Looking at the timing breakdown, the form took about 148 seconds with 20 calls—already fairly efficient at 2-10 steps per action. The mail step ate up 300 seconds though, mostly spent fighting UI gates in the webmail to retrieve the TAN, with around 45 act calls needed just to navigate sliders, checkboxes, and buttons per message.

After that, things fell apart: a sign error occurred because the summary check failed, then the session expired mid-task, forcing a full wizard restart from scratch. This happened twice more before the budget ran out, revealing that both the mail-retrieval gates (66% of total time) and the portal's aggressive session timeout were the two biggest bottlenecks.

I've traced the a10 submission timeline: the bid form itself only took 148s, but the webmail TAN-fetching step ate 300s fighting UI gates and timeouts, then signing failed on a unit-price mismatch and the portal session expired, forcing re-logins that burned the remaining budget. I'll send these findings to hackathon-af.

input.message:
a10-full submit analysis (rfq-run-gyuc5vmv/submit/session.jsonl, per call: think time, run time, steps):

1. Wizard: 0–148 s, 20 calls, already multi-step: act carried 2–10 steps each (configurator chains like 10 steps in one call, 5.6–9.2 s run). Think 2–4 s/call. So "field by field" is NOT the problem in a10; the wizard phase is OK (one 22 s act on Katalognummer).

2. Webmail TAN retrieval: 148–448 s = 300 s, ~45 calls (66% of the submit). Pattern: list gate, per-message gate and "Nachrichtentext (Original)" gate, each slider+checkbox+button. ~12 clicks failed with "Locator.click: Timeout 5000ms" (≈5.3 s each, ~65 s burned) and ~10 were "BLOCKED by <section id=mail-original-gate / mail-list-gate / div role=dialog>", meaning it clicked the target before the gate was passed or a dialog closed. It re-passed the same gates repeatedly (drag+check+click sequences ~15 times).
   Suggestions: pass the list gate during pre-warm; act could auto-detect "BLOCKED by <gate>" and return the gate's controls instead of the click error; a shorter click timeout (2 s) on BLOCKED cases.

3. 451 s: sign → "ERROR (not shown on the summary: ['1692.74','1906.85','2614.68',…])". Sonnet passed unit prices as other_values; the summary shows only the total. Prompt (or tool) should pass only net_total unless the summary is known to show more.

4. 454 s+: the portal session had expired during the 300 s in the webmail → login → consent → wizard restarted from step 1. Sonnet refilled with 20-step and one 59-step act (35 s), expired again at 529 s and 584 s → 600 s budget out. So: keep the portal tab alive during the mail phase (or do the webmail part right after "TAN anfordern" fast enough), and when a re-login lands on step 1, the 59-step refill works but needs the session to last.

Bottom line: with the webmail gate handling + no false sign refusal + no expiry, this submit would have signed at ~455 s; with the list gate pre-passed and fewer blocked clicks, maybe ~250 s.

content.text:
I analyzed the lab's newest full run (a10) and sent the findings to hackathon-af, so here's the answer to "still 7–8 minutes".

Research is now fast: about 4 minutes with p13 (241 s in this run). The submit took up to 10 minutes and still failed. Breakdown:
- **Filling in the bid form: about 2.5 minutes, and already efficient**, with whole form steps per call.
- **Fetching the TAN from the webmail: 5 minutes.** Sonnet fights the webmail's gates (slider, checkbox, button on the list, on each message and on the "original text" view). About 12 clicks timed out, and about 10 were blocked by overlays.
- **Signing was then refused** by the tool's own check, because Sonnet asked it to check unit prices that the summary page doesn't show.
- **Meanwhile the portal session had expired**, so the bid form restarted, and the 600 s budget ran out.

The fixes are all in the lab's submit code: pass the webmail gates while research is running, keep the portal session alive, and check only the total when signing. With those, this run would have signed after about 4–7 minutes of submit. I'm leaving the implementation to hackathon-af, as it asked, and will run its next variant through the same analysis once it's done.

cat > /Users/simon/hackathon/urltest/submit_timeline.py <<'EOF'
"""Submit phase of a lab run: per call think/run time and steps, phase totals (form site vs mail site), and the
failure patterns that cost time (click timeouts, BLOCKED by overlays, re-logins, sign refusals).

    python3 urltest/submit_timeline.py lab/runs/<run-dir> [--calls]
"""
import datetime, json, re, sys
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

run = Path(sys.argv[1])
work = re.search(r"Workdir (\S+)", (run / "log.txt").read_text())
if not work:
    sys.exit("no 'Workdir' line in the log")
sess = next(Path(work.group(1)).glob("submit*/session.jsonl"), None)
if not sess:
    sys.exit(f"no submit session under {work.group(1)}")
rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open(sess) if l.startswith("{")]
ts = lambda d: datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(d["timestamp"].replace("Z", "+00:00"))
res, rt = {}, {}
for d in rows:
    if d.get("type") == "user" and isinstance(d.get("message", {}).get("content"), list):
        for b in d["message"]["content"]:
            if b.get("type") == "tool_result":
                c = b.get("content")
                res[b["tool_use_id"]] = c if isinstance(c, str) else " ".join(x.get("text", "") for x in c if isinstance(x, dict))
                rt[b["tool_use_id"]] = ts(d)
t0 = min(ts(d) for d in rows if "timestamp" in d)
site_time, pat = Counter(), Counter()
prev, calls = t0, []
for d in rows:
    if d.get("type") != "assistant":
        continue
    for b in d["message"].get("content", []):
        if b.get("type") != "tool_use":
            continue
        st, en = ts(d), rt.get(b["id"], ts(d))
        name, inp, out = b["name"].split("__")[-1], b["input"], res.get(b["id"], "")
        site = inp.get("site", "-")
        site_time[site] += max(0, (en - prev).total_seconds())
        pat["click timeout (5 s)"] += out.count("Timeout 5000ms")
        pat["BLOCKED by overlay/gate"] += out.count("BLOCKED by")
        pat["login"] += name == "login"
        pat["sign refused"] += name == "sign" and out.lstrip('{"result":').startswith("ERROR")
        calls.append(f"{(st - t0).total_seconds():6.0f}s think {(st - prev).total_seconds():4.1f}s run "
                     f"{(en - st).total_seconds():5.1f}s {name:12} {site:14} "
                     f"{len(inp.get('steps', [])) if name == 'act' else '':>3} {out[:90]!r}")
        prev = en
total = (prev - t0).total_seconds()
print(f"submit session: {total:.0f} s, {len(calls)} calls  ({sess})")
for s, t in site_time.most_common():
    print(f"  time on {s:16} {t:5.0f} s")
print("  " + ", ".join(f"{k}: {v}" for k, v in pat.items()))
if "--calls" in sys.argv:
    print("\n".join(calls))
EOF

11	Claude Code (2.1.293 binary) caps every MCP tool description at 4096 characters, or 16384 for deferred tools loaded through ToolSearch, and appends "… [truncated]". It is configurable with `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_MCP_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH` (also applies to MCP server instructions).
12	
13	Found 2026-10-11 in the RFQ lab: the `record` tool in web_tools.py carries the full evidence JSON schema (21,454 chars). The cut fell inside the messages kind, so Sonnet never saw the Message fields and guessed. Every run had 14–17 rejected record calls (about half of all record calls).
14	
15	Verified with `claude -p --model sonnet` against the MCP server: default ends mid-ConditionRule with "[truncated]"; with the env at 40000 the full schema arrives. urltest/u3 (env line in claude_env) cut rejections to 1 per run, quality 100 on public-1 and combo; time and cost unchanged (n=2).
16	
17	Follow-up u4 (same day): rendering the schema compactly from the pydantic models (`name*: type - description`, 21.4k → 8.7k chars) kept rejections at 1 and lowered est. cost to $1.46–1.59 (avg $1.53 vs $1.77 baseline, 3 runs, all 100). Patch: urltest/compact-schema.patch, sent to both threads.
18	
19	Also measured that day: a prompt-only "open same-kind pages by URL" hint made no difference (Sonnet already navigates by URL and writes its own fetch() scrapers in browser_evaluate), and an in-browser fetch() tool was worse (314–466 s). The ERP worker is the critical path in every parallel run.
20	
21	**Why:** a silent cap hides schema from the model; it looks like model sloppiness.
22	**How to apply:** in any agent that ships long MCP tool descriptions, set `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_MCP_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH` in the claude subprocess env, or keep descriptions short (urltest/u4 tests a compact 8.7k schema rendering). 23

content.text: Was the url fetching approach promising?

content.thinking: This is just a direct question I can answer now — no need for more work, just summarizing what I found from fetching the URL.

content.text:
Not as a speedup. As a safety finding it was the most important thing to come out of today. Every variant below scored 100 unless marked:

| Variant | What it tried | Runs | Time | Est. cost (avg) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| u0 baseline | nothing extra | 3 | 220–358 s | $1.77 | reference |
| u1 | prompt hint "open same-kind pages by URL, it's cheaper" | 3 | 275–299 s | $1.62 | no real difference |
| u2 | in-browser `fetch` tool with a click fallback | 3 | 314–466 s | $1.98 | worse |
| u5 | prompt: read many pages of a kind in one fetch script | 1 | 170 s | $1.22 | fast, but **read around gates** |
| u6 | same, but open one page of each kind in the browser first | 3 | 233–362 s | $1.55 | fair-play-safe, cost-neutral |

**Why it didn't speed things up:** Sonnet already does it on its own. In every run it goes to URLs directly and writes its own `fetch()` scripts (2–19 per run), so a hint changes nothing. A dedicated tool only adds calls, because Sonnet uses it on top of its own scripts.

**Why u5 looked fast:** it fetched mail messages without opening them, which skips their per-message gate. With the fair-play rule in place (u6), most of that speed goes away.

**What made it worth testing:** the same behavior already happens unprompted. In 4 of 7 normal runs, Sonnet's own scripts read gated mail messages around their gates. That's a reviewer-rejection risk in every thread's agent. The u6 rule ("open one page of each kind in the browser first") fixes it at no cost. Both threads have adopted it, and `urltest/gate_audit.py` checks runs for it.

The real speed problem is elsewhere: research (the ERP worker) and especially submitting, where fetching the TAN through the gated webmail took about 5 minutes in the last full run.

I'm still paused otherwise.

content.text:
The goal is cleared, so the reminders will stop. Here are the main insights from today, most important first.

**1. Submitting is the biggest risk, not research**
- Research is solved: explore's p13 takes about 4 minutes and scores 100 every time, including on the changed-looking sites.
- Submitting has **never signed on changed-looking sites (0 of 8 attempts)**, and the private run uses different sites. An unsigned bid scores nothing.
- In the latest full run (a10), filling in the form took about 2.5 minutes and was efficient. **Fetching the TAN through the gated webmail took 5 minutes**: about 12 clicks timed out and about 10 were blocked by overlays. Signing was then refused by the tool's own check, and the portal session had expired, so the form restarted and the run ran out of time.
- The fixes (pass the webmail gates during research, keep the portal session alive, check only the total when signing) are in the lab thread's hands.

**2. Fair-play risk was already present and is now fixed**
- Sonnet writes its own `fetch()` scripts in every run, and in 4 of 7 normal runs they read mail messages around their per-message gates. That's what reviewers reject.
- The rule "open one page of each kind in the browser first" fixes it at no extra cost. Both threads have adopted it.
- `urltest/gate_audit.py` checks any run for the problem. Run it before submitting.

**3. Two silent bugs made the agent guess or accept wrong numbers**
- **Truncated schema:** Claude Code cuts MCP tool descriptions at 16,384 characters, so Sonnet never saw half the data schema and about 15 save calls per run were rejected. One setting (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_MCP_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH`) brought that down to 1.
- **Number check gap:** a value like "73.697" sent as a string skipped the ambiguity check, so a 1000× price error could get through with any model. Fixed, and adopted by both threads.

**4. Cost: the compact schema is the one clear win**
Writing the same schema in a short readable form makes research about 14–17% cheaper at the same quality (on p13: $1.86 → $1.56). The lab thread is putting it into its next variant.

**5. Ideas that didn't pan out**
- **URL fetching**, whether as a prompt hint or as a tool, didn't help: Sonnet already does it. The fast version only looked fast because it skipped gates.
- **Haiku** is 20× cheaper per token, but only 3 of 5 runs scored 100. Accuracy ranks first, so it's out.

**6. Privacy**
A local test submit put your Gmail address into a bid on the public-1 tender portal. Locally, Claude Code always tells the model the account e-mail. The lab fixed the prompt so the contact address comes from the webmail, and in the sandbox no account e-mail is available. Ask the organizers if you want the address removed from the portal.

**What to do next:** get the submit step to sign reliably on changed-looking sites within about 5 minutes. Then take p13 + compact schema + the lab's submit, check it with the gate audit and confirm the contact address, and only then consider a sandbox test run.

All of this is saved to memory. The tools are in `urltest/`: `analyze.py`, `gate_audit.py`, `submit_timeline.py`.

content.thinking:
Right, there's already a `login(site)` tool that fills credentials generically and submits — this fits the rule that helpers can mechanically fill forms, as long as the model itself decides whether and where to log in. Earlier research workers typically handled logins this way too.

Cookie consent walls are similar — a code helper clicking "accept necessary cookies" counts as filling a form/gate, which is allowed, though trickier things like robot checks or sliders are riskier to automate. As for actual time savings, login only costs about 10-20 seconds per site, so with a few sites in parallel and occasional re-logins from session timeouts, the saved time is modest — maybe 10-15 seconds on the critical path — since the bigger costs were webmail gates and session expirations, not login itself.

I'm realizing research workers log in via Playwright clicks too, and ERP specifically had two re-logins due to short session timeouts — that's a real, measurable gain if I extend the existing login helper there. For generality I'd need to handle password field detection across frames, two-step logins (username then password on a separate page), SSO patterns, and varying submit mechanisms, with a fallback to model-driven clicks and verification that the password field disappeared and the URL changed. I'll answer honestly with the numbers, suggest adding the login helper to research workers since the ERP re-login savings are concrete, and ask if they'd like me to test it rather than starting work unprompted.

content.text:
You're right: login doesn't need the model clicking around. It's a mechanical form fill, and the rules explicitly allow helpers that "fill forms" and "retry", as long as the model decides when and where to log in.

**It partly exists already.** The lab's submit step has a `login(site)` tool that does it in code; in the a10 log it shows up as "Submitted the login." in one call. **The research workers don't have it.** They log in with Playwright: fill the fields, click "Anmelden", then a snapshot. That's 3–5 turns per login, about 10–20 s.

**How much it would save:**
- **First login:** small. All 4 sites log in at the same time, so at most 10–15 s.
- **Re-logins: that's where it counts.** Per the spec, the ERP has a short session timeout, and the ERP worker is the slowest part of every run. In some runs it logged in again 2–3 times, about 15 s each, all on the slowest path. In the submit, an expired session meant the form restarted, which cost minutes.

**A generic login helper would try the common patterns in order:**
1. Find a password field anywhere on the page, including iframes. The username field is the nearest text or e-mail field before it in the same form.
2. Fill both with the credentials from the run's access list.
3. Submit: press Enter, or click the submit button of that form.
4. **Two-step login** (no password field yet): fill the username, submit, wait for the password field, repeat.
5. **Check it worked:** the password field is gone and the URL changed. Report "session expired" as its own case.
6. If none of that works, it says so and the model logs in by clicking, as now.

**Where I'd draw the line:** a cookie wall's "accept necessary cookies" button is still a normal form, so including it is fine. But **sliders, "not a robot" boxes and code gates should stay with the model in the browser**, since that's exactly what the fair-play reviewers look for.

**The bigger version of your idea:** have code check whether the session is still alive, and log back in before a worker even notices. In the a10 submit, that alone would have saved the restarted form and probably the whole run.

Do you want me to test it? It would be p13 + the login helper for the research workers, with the session refresh, A/B against plain p13 on the normal and changed-looking sites, research only, one run at a time. That's about 4 runs and 20–25 minutes. The submit-side version I'd hand to hackathon-af, since it owns that code.

I notice almost no actual link clicks happen in practice—the clicks are really buttons for cookie walls, popups, download bars, dropdowns, gates like checkboxes or sliders, and logins, plus unsafe code calls for gates that aren't counted. So the research already sidesteps link clicking, with only 20-30 non-navigation actions per run, all of which are buttons or gates that can't simply be replaced by direct URLs.

content.text:
That's already almost how it works. In those two recent research runs, Sonnet made only **20–30 actions that weren't navigation**, out of about 140–170 tool calls. **Almost none were link clicks.** Here's what they were:

| Kind | Count | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Buttons | 9–11 | "Notwendige Cookies akzeptieren" (cookie wall), "Schließen" (closing popups), closing the download bar, the "Verfahrensakte" dropdown |
| Login forms | 2–4 | username, password, ERP "Empfangsnummer" (receipt number) |
| Gates | 3–5 | "Ich bin kein Roboter" checkbox, "Zum Entsperren ziehen" slider, terms checkbox and radio button, typing the document code |
| Search fields | 1–2 | ERP "Bezeichnung enthält" |

Sonnet goes to pages by URL already, and it even writes its own scripts that fetch pages by URL.

**What's left can't be replaced by following a link:**
- **Cookie walls and login:** these are forms. A helper could do them in code (the login helper from my last message), saving a few turns per site and per re-login.
- **Popups and overlays:** they sit on top of the page and block it. Going to a URL doesn't remove them; they reappear.
- **Gates (sliders, checkboxes, codes):** they have to be passed in the browser, or the fair-play reviewers can reject the entry. Skipping them by URL is exactly what u5 did.
- **The bid form:** its progress is kept in the session and the selections depend on each other, so it can't be walked through by links.

**So clicking isn't where the time goes.** With about 25 clicks out of about 150 calls, removing every click would save maybe 10–15%. The time is in the **number of turns**: reading pages, recording evidence, waiting for other workers. Each turn is about 2–4 s of model thinking. In the submit step, it's the webmail gates and the expired portal session.

**Of your idea, the parts worth doing are:**
1. a **login + cookie-wall helper**, plus **keeping sessions alive**. This mainly avoids re-logins on the slowest path (ERP) and the restarted bid form in the submit;
2. letting the model **chain several actions in one call**, like `act` in the submit tools, for example close popup → open dropdown → read, instead of one turn each.

I can test (1) for research if you want, about 20–25 minutes. The submit-side version belongs to hackathon-af.

Right, for reading they don't:
- **Popups and the download bar:** they only cover the page visually. The text underneath is still in the page, and `read` and Sonnet's own scripts get it without closing anything. Sonnet closes them out of habit, because it works from screenshots and snapshots like a user.

**How to test it, generally and without site knowledge:**
- **Prompt:** "Don't close popups or open menus to read: read the page text and links directly. Interact only when a page doesn't give you its content otherwise."
- **Helper:** login + cookie wall in one call, plus refreshing the session before it expires (the ERP re-logins).

content.text: but then the idea is easy just dump all form actions and urls and then the model just navigates to an url form action

content.thinking:
This idea resembles the "Beyond Browsing" API-agent and htmlswarm approaches, condensing HTML into links and form actions so the model just picks a URL or fills a field — fewer tokens, deterministic, fast, and generic since forms and links cover most interactions.

But there are real risks: JS-driven controls (buttons with handlers, SPA fetch calls, sliders, dialogs) won't show up as static forms or links, so those interactions get missed entirely. The gates themselves are JS-based, and directly submitting their underlying form fields raises a grey-zone concern about whether the model is genuinely passing checks or just faking them, especially given earlier guidance that gates should be passed in the browser, not circumvented. There's also the wizard's server-side validation, which seems to depend on real JS-computed tokens or input events, meaning plain HTTP POSTs might fail the same way pure field-setting did before — plus hidden fields, decoys, and CSRF tokens to handle correctly.

Looking at prior evidence, I'm weighing a hybrid approach: use a lightweight links-and-forms view as the default way of observing pages, falling back to the full browser only for JS-only controls or gates. But I recall that when a similar fetch-based tool was added alongside full browsing before, the model just kept using its old approach instead of switching, so simply adding the tool won't produce the efficiency gain — it would need to become the primary interface, which risks breaking generality on JS-heavy sites. I'm leaning toward framing this as a scoped research experiment: a "page" tool that returns readable text plus numbered links and forms (with fields, options, and target actions), supporting simple open and submit actions routed through the same logged-in browser session.

For form submission specifically, I think using the real browser to fill fields by name and submit preserves JS semantics while still being a single action — essentially what `act` already does. I'll present this assessment concisely and offer to run the experiment.

content.text:
That's a coherent design: show the model each page as **text + a list of links + a list of forms** (fields, options, target), and let it choose "open link 7" or "submit form 2 with these values". The code turns that into requests. It's close to what research papers call API-based or distilled-DOM web agents. It's allowed as long as the model picks every step, since the code only extracts a page the model chose. Here's how I'd rate it, based on what we've measured:

**Where it works well:**
- **Reading (research):** most pages are plain links, lists and GET searches (the ERP search, for example, works with URL parameters). Here it would save tokens and turns.
- **Login and cookie walls:** real HTML forms, one "submit form" step each.

**Where it breaks:**
1. **Controls run by JavaScript:** buttons that fetch data in the background, sliders, dialogs, menus built by scripts. They don't show up as a `<form>` or `<a>`, so a static list misses them. On the private sites ("different software") this could be most of the page, if they're built as single-page apps.
2. **Gates:** a slider or "not a robot" box is technically also just a request. Sending it directly instead of passing it in the browser is exactly what reviewers reject.
3. **The bid form:** progress is kept server-side and values are computed by script. An earlier test found that values set by script weren't accepted ("Bieter nicht registriert"), so a pure HTTP submission probably fails there.
4. **Previous evidence:**
   - htmlswarm (shortened HTML in, one action out) never produced a bid, but it used the much weaker DeepSeek.
   - My `fetch` tool (u2) didn't help, because Sonnet kept its own way of working and used the tool on top.
   - **So it only pays off if it replaces the browser view as the default, not as an extra tool.** That's also the risky part.

**What I'd test: a hybrid**
- **Default view:** each page as text + numbered links + forms (with their fields and options), read from the real browser tab. That way pages built by scripts are included, which a raw HTTP download wouldn't give.
- **Actions:**
  - `open(link)`;
  - `submit(form, values)`: fills the form in the real browser and submits it, so the page's scripts and server-side state behave normally;
  - a fallback to the normal browser for anything that's neither a link nor a form;
  - gates always in the browser.
